sections.title: Exponential functions
sections.html:
An exponential function has the variable in the exponent and a fixed positive base that is not 1.

\[f(x) = a^x, \qquad a > 0,\; a \neq 1,\; x \in \mathbb{R}\]

Why the base rules? a = 1 gives the flat line y = 1 (not exponential). A negative base fails for values like x = 0.5, since (−2)^0.5 = √(−2) is not real.

Evaluating: the three tricks

Exponent Rule Example
negative flip the base: a^(−x) = 1/a^x 2^(−3) = 1/2³ = 1/8 = 0.125
zero anything (allowed) to the 0 is 1 2^0 = 1
fraction 1/2 square root: a^(1/2) = √a 2^0.5 = √2 ≈ 1.4142

WorkedWorked: Examples 2 and 3 from the notes

x f(x) = 2^x g(x) = (1/2)^x
−3 1/8 = 0.125 8
0 1 1
0.5 √2 ≈ 1.4142 √(1/2) ≈ 0.7071
−π 1/2^π ≈ 0.1133 2^π ≈ 8.8250

Notice g(x) = (1/2)^x = 2^(−x). So g is just f with x replaced by −x: every value of f appears in g, mirrored. That is why their graphs are reflections of each other in the y-axis.

Calculator tip: for e^x use the e^x key (usually SHIFT + ln). For a^(−π), type the brackets: 2 ^ ( − π ).

sections.title: Graphs and properties of y = a^x
sections.html:
Every basic exponential graph passes through (0, 1), stays above the x-axis, and has the x-axis (y = 0) as its horizontal asymptote. The base only decides whether it rises or falls.

Table of values from the notes

x −3 −2 −1 0 1 2 3
2^x 1/8 1/4 1/2 1 2 4 8
(1/2)^x 8 4 2 1 1/2 1/4 1/8
Property a > 1 (e.g. 2^x, e^x) 0 < a < 1 (e.g. (1/2)^x, 0.3^x)
Domain (−∞, +∞) (−∞, +∞)
Range (0, +∞) (0, +∞)
y-intercept (0, 1) (0, 1)
x-intercept none none
Behaviour increasing (growth) decreasing (decay)
Horizontal asymptote y = 0, on the left (x → −∞) y = 0, on the right (x → +∞)
One-to-one? yes yes

How to tell growth from decay quickly: look at the base after simplifying. 3^x, 1.5^x, e^x grow. (3/4)^x, 0.3^x, e^(−x) = (1/e)^x decay. A base written as 2^(−x) is decay, because 2^(−x) = (1/2)^x.

Laws of exponents (a, b > 0)

Law Rule Quick example
Product a^x · a^y = a^(x+y) 2³ · 2⁴ = 2⁷
Quotient a^x / a^y = a^(x−y) 5⁶ / 5² = 5⁴
Negative power a^(−x) = 1/a^x = (1/a)^x 3^(−2) = 1/9
Power of a product (ab)^x = a^x b^x (2·3)² = 4·9 = 36
Power of a power (a^x)^y = a^(xy) (2³)² = 2⁶ = 64
Power of a quotient (a/b)^x = a^x / b^x (2/3)³ = 8/27
Zero power a^0 = 1 e^0 = 1
Squares |a²| = |a|² = a² |(−3)²| = 9

Using the laws to solve an equation: write both sides with the same base, then set the exponents equal (this works because a^x is one-to-one).

\[4^{x+1} = 8^{x} \;\Rightarrow\; 2^{2(x+1)} = 2^{3x} \;\Rightarrow\; 2x + 2 = 3x \;\Rightarrow\; x = 2\]

sections.title: Transformations and the natural base e
sections.html:
Any function like h(x) = A·a^(x − c) + k is the parent graph a^x moved around. The horizontal asymptote moves to y = k, and that is the first thing to write down.

Change to f(x) = a^x New function Effect on the graph
x → −x a^(−x) reflect in the y-axis
multiply by −1 −a^x reflect in the x-axis
x → x + c (c > 0) a^(x + c) shift c units left
x → x − c (c > 0) a^(x − c) shift c units right
add c (c > 0) a^x + c shift c units up (HA becomes y = c)
subtract c (c > 0) a^x − c shift c units down (HA becomes y = −c)

Order that never fails: (1) reflections, (2) horizontal shift, (3) vertical shift. Inside the exponent, factor out the minus first: a^(−x + 1) = a^(−(x − 1)), which is a reflection in the y-axis and then a shift right 1, not left.

The natural base e

e = 2.718281828… is an irrational number, like π. f(x) = e^x is the natural exponential function. Because e > 1, it behaves like 2^x: increasing, through (0, 1), HA y = 0.

x −3 −2 −1 −0.5 0 0.5 1 2
e^x 0.0498 0.1353 0.3679 0.6065 1 1.6487 2.7183 7.3891

WorkedWorked: Example 4, h(x) = 2 − e^(x+3)

Parent f(x) = e^x.

  1. Reflect in the x-axis: h₁(x) = −e^x.
  2. Shift 3 units left: h₂(x) = −e^(x+3).
  3. Shift 2 units up: h(x) = 2 − e^(x+3).
Feature f(x) = e^x h(x) = 2 − e^(x+3)
HA y = 0 y = 2
Range (0, ∞) (−∞, 2) (graph is below its HA because of the reflection)
y-intercept (0, 1) (0, 2 − e³) ≈ (0, −18.09)
x-intercept none e^(x+3) = 2 gives x = ln 2 − 3 ≈ −2.31
Behaviour increasing decreasing

WorkedWorked: Example 5, h(x) = 2^(−x+1) − 3

Parent f(x) = 2^x.

  1. Reflect in the y-axis: h₁(x) = 2^(−x).
  2. Shift 1 unit right: h₂(x) = h₁(x − 1) = 2^(−(x−1)) = 2^(−x+1).
  3. Shift 3 units down: h(x) = 2^(−x+1) − 3.
Feature f(x) = 2^x h(x) = 2^(−x+1) − 3
HA y = 0 y = −3
Range (0, ∞) (−3, ∞)
y-intercept (0, 1) 2¹ − 3 = (0, −1)
x-intercept none 2^(1−x) = 3 gives x = 1 − log₂ 3 ≈ −0.585
Behaviour increasing decreasing (the y-reflection turned growth into decay)

Sketch checklist: dashed HA at y = k, plot the y-intercept, plot one point either side, then draw the curve hugging the HA on the correct side.

sections.title: Logarithmic functions
sections.html:
A logarithm answers one question: "what power do I raise a to, to get x?" Because a^x passes the Horizontal Line Test (it is one-to-one), it has an inverse, and that inverse is logₐ x.

\[y = \log_a x \iff x = a^y, \qquad x > 0,\; a > 0,\; a \neq 1\]

Converting between the two forms (the base stays the base; the log is the exponent)

Log form Exponential form Read it as
log₂ 8 = 3 2³ = 8 2 to the 3 is 8
log₁₀ 10000 = 4 10⁴ = 10000
log₄ (1/64) = −3 4^(−3) = 1/64
log₅ 1 = 0 5⁰ = 1
log₉ 3 = 1/2 9^(1/2) = 3
ln e = 1 e¹ = e

Evaluating without a calculator: write x as a power of the base. log₃ 81 = log₃ 3⁴ = 4. log₂ (1/8) = log₂ 2^(−3) = −3.

Common and natural logs

  • Common log: log x means log₁₀ x (the LOG key).
  • Natural log: ln x means logₑ x, the inverse of e^x (the LN key).
\[y = \ln x \iff x = e^y\]

Why the domain is x > 0: a^y is always positive, so you can never get 0 or a negative number out of it. That is why log₂(0), log₂(−4) and ln(−1) are undefined.

Domain of a log with an expression inside: set the inside > 0 and solve.

Function Inside > 0 Domain
log₃ (x − 2) x − 2 > 0 (2, ∞)
ln (5 − x) 5 − x > 0 (−∞, 5)
log (2x + 6) 2x + 6 > 0 (−3, ∞)
ln (x²) x² > 0 all reals except 0

checks.q: Rewrite in the other form: (a) log₅ 125 = 3 (b) 2^(−4) = 1/16 (c) e^x = 10.

sections.title: Graphs and properties of y = logₐ x
sections.html:
The log graph is the exponential graph reflected in the line y = x. Every point (p, q) on a^x becomes (q, p) on logₐ x, so (0, 1) becomes (1, 0) and the horizontal asymptote y = 0 becomes the vertical asymptote x = 0.

y = 2^x (−2, 1/4) (−1, 1/2) (0, 1) (1, 2) (2, 4) (3, 8)
y = log₂ x (1/4, −2) (1/2, −1) (1, 0) (2, 1) (4, 2) (8, 3)

Domain and range swap

f(x) = a^x g(x) = logₐ x
Domain (−∞, +∞) (0, +∞)
Range (0, +∞) (−∞, +∞)
Property a > 1 (log₂ x, ln x, log x) 0 < a < 1 (log₁/₂ x)
Domain (0, +∞) (0, +∞)
Range (−∞, +∞) (−∞, +∞)
x-intercept (1, 0) (1, 0)
y-intercept none none
Behaviour increasing decreasing
Vertical asymptote x = 0 (y-axis), f → −∞ as x → 0⁺ x = 0 (y-axis), f → +∞ as x → 0⁺
One-to-one? yes yes

Sign of logₐ x when a > 1: negative for 0 < x < 1, zero at x = 1, positive for x > 1. You can see this in Example 7 below.

Example 7: f(x) = log₃ x (calculator: ln x ÷ ln 3)

x 0.001 0.1 0.5 1 1.5 2 3 4 9 75
log₃ x −6.288 −2.096 −0.631 0 0.369 0.631 1 1.262 2 3.930

Transformations of log graphs: the same rules as section 3, but now the vertical asymptote moves. For y = logₐ(x − c) + k: VA x = c, domain (c, ∞), and the point (1, 0) moves to (1 + c, k).

Example: y = ln(x + 2) − 1 is ln x shifted 2 left and 1 down. VA x = −2, domain (−2, ∞), key point (−1, −1). x-intercept: ln(x + 2) = 1 gives x = e − 2 ≈ 0.718.

y = log₂(x − 3) + 1. Give the VA, domain, x-intercept and the image of the point (1, 0).

sections.title: Laws of logarithms and change of base
sections.html:
The log laws are the exponent laws in disguise: logs turn multiplication into addition, division into subtraction and powers into multiplication. They hold for x, y > 0.

Law logₐ form ln form Comes from
Log of 1 logₐ 1 = 0 ln 1 = 0 a⁰ = 1
Log of the base logₐ a = 1 ln e = 1 a¹ = a
Product logₐ(xy) = logₐ x + logₐ y ln(xy) = ln x + ln y a^x a^y = a^(x+y)
Quotient logₐ(x/y) = logₐ x − logₐ y ln(x/y) = ln x − ln y a^x / a^y = a^(x−y)
Power logₐ(b^x) = x logₐ b ln(b^x) = x ln b (a^x)^y = a^(xy)
Inverse 1 a^(logₐ x) = x e^(ln x) = x, x > 0 inverse functions
Inverse 2 logₐ(a^x) = x ln(e^x) = x, all x inverse functions

Change of base (how your calculator does any base)

\[\log_a b = \frac{\ln b}{\ln a} = \frac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}, \qquad c > 0,\; c \neq 1\]

Example: log₇ 65 = ln 65 / ln 7 = 4.1744 / 1.9459 ≈ 2.145.

Things that are NOT laws (these are the classic mark-losers)

  • log(x + y) ≠ log x + log y. There is no rule for the log of a sum.
  • log x · log y ≠ log(xy).
  • (log x)/(log y) ≠ log(x/y). (It is log_y x, by change of base.)
  • (ln x)² ≠ 2 ln x. Only ln(x²) = 2 ln x.

Expanding (break one log into many)

\[\log_2\!\left(\frac{8x^3}{y}\right) = \log_2 8 + \log_2 x^3 - \log_2 y = 3 + 3\log_2 x - \log_2 y\]

Condensing (many logs into one): powers first, then combine.

\[2\ln x + \ln 3 - \ln y = \ln x^2 + \ln 3 - \ln y = \ln\!\left(\frac{3x^2}{y}\right)\]

Solving equations: two moves

  1. Variable in the exponent → take ln (or log) of both sides and bring the power down. 3^x = 20 gives x ln 3 = ln 20, so x = ln 20 / ln 3 ≈ 2.727. And e^(2x) = 7 gives 2x = ln 7, so x ≈ 0.973.
  2. Variable inside a log → condense to one log, then rewrite in exponential form. Always check the answer in the original equation (the inside of every log must be > 0).
\[\log_2 x + \log_2 (x-2) = 3 \Rightarrow \log_2[x(x-2)] = 3 \Rightarrow x^2 - 2x = 8 \Rightarrow (x-4)(x+2)=0\]

x = 4 works. x = −2 is rejected because log₂(−2) is undefined.

sections.title: Exam checklist, traps and practice
sections.html:
For any transformed exponential or log in the test, run through this list in order.

  • Name the parent (a^x, e^x, logₐ x or ln x) and whether it grows or decays
  • List the transformations in order: reflections → horizontal shift → vertical shift
  • Exponential: write the HA y = k and the range (above or below k?)
  • Log: write the VA x = c and the domain (inside > 0)
  • y-intercept: put x = 0 (logs may have none)
  • x-intercept: set y = 0 and solve with logs or exponentials (may have none)
  • Sketch: dashed asymptote, intercepts, one extra point each side, curve hugging the asymptote

Traps that lose marks

  • Reading a^(x + c) as a shift right. +c inside is left.
  • Missing the factor-out in a^(−x + 1) = a^(−(x − 1)): it is a shift right 1.
  • Treating −2^x as (−2)^x. The minus is outside: −(2^x).
  • Saying an exponential's range is (0, ∞) after a vertical shift or an x-axis reflection.
  • Using log(x + y) = log x + log y. There is no such law.
  • Keeping a solution that puts a negative number or 0 inside a log.
  • Forgetting the brackets on the calculator: type log(65) ÷ log(7), and 2^(−π).

Practice questions (answers below — cover them first)

  1. Evaluate to 3 d.p.: (a) 3^(−√2) (b) e^(−1.5) (c) (2/5)^(−2).

sections.title: What a rational function is
sections.html:
A rational function is one polynomial divided by another. Its domain is every real number except the x-values that make the denominator zero.

\[f(x) = \frac{N(x)}{D(x)}, \qquad D(x) \text{ not the zero polynomial}\]

Domain in 2 steps

  1. Set the denominator = 0 and solve.
  2. Write the domain as all reals except those values, e.g. ℝ \ {−2, 2} or ℝ − {−2, 2}.

Use the original denominator for the domain, before cancelling anything. A cancelled factor still makes the original function undefined.

Function Denominator = 0 Domain
1/x x = 0 ℝ \ {0}
2x/(3x² + 1) 3x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution ℝ (all reals)
(x² + x − 2)/(x² − x − 6) (x + 2)(x − 3) = 0 ℝ \ {−2, 3}
(3x³ + 7x² + 2)/(−2x³ + 16) x³ = 8 ℝ \ {2}

Notation you must be able to read

Symbol Meaning
x → a⁻ x approaches a from the left (values just below a)
x → a⁺ x approaches a from the right (values just above a)
x → +∞ x increases without bound
x → −∞ x decreases without bound
f(x) → +∞ as x → a⁺ f shoots up as x comes towards a from the right
f(x) → b as x → ±∞ f levels off towards the value b far left/right

Example from the notes: for f(x) = 1/x, f(x) → −∞ as x → 0⁻ (f(−0.001) = −1000) and f(x) → +∞ as x → 0⁺ (f(0.001) = 1000).

sections.title: Vertical asymptotes and holes
sections.html:
Factor top and bottom first. A factor that cancels gives a hole. A factor left in the denominator gives a vertical asymptote (VA).

Method

  1. Factor N(x) and D(x) completely.
  2. Cancel any common factor (x − a). That x = a is a hole.
  3. Hole's y-value: put x = a into the simplified function.
  4. Set the simplified denominator = 0. Each solution is a VA, written as the line x = a.

The line x = a is a vertical asymptote when f(x) → +∞ or −∞ as x → a from the left or the right. The graph never crosses a vertical asymptote.

Vertical asymptote Hole
Comes from factor left in the denominator after cancelling factor that cancels top and bottom
Graph does shoots to ±∞ beside it has a single missing point
Drawn as dashed vertical line open circle at (a, y)
Written as x = a the point (a, b)

WorkedWorked example (Week 7, Example 5)

\[f(x) = \frac{x^2 + x - 2}{x^2 - x - 6} = \frac{(x - 1)(x + 2)}{(x + 2)(x - 3)} = \frac{x - 1}{x - 3}, \quad x \neq -2\]
  • (x + 2) cancels, so there is a hole at x = −2: y = (−2 − 1)/(−2 − 3) = −3/−5 = 0.6, so the hole is at (−2, 0.6).
  • The simplified denominator x − 3 = 0 gives the VA x = 3.
  • x = −2 is not a VA, even though it made the original denominator zero.

More from the notes

  • 2x²/(x² − 1) = 2x²/[(x + 1)(x − 1)]: nothing cancels, so the VAs are x = −1 and x = 1.
  • 2x/(3x² + 1): 3x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution, so there is no VA.
  • (x² − 9)/(x² − 2x − 3) = (x + 3)/(x + 1), x ≠ 3: hole at (3, 3/2), VA x = −1.

sections.title: Horizontal asymptotes
sections.html:
Compare the degree of the top (n) with the degree of the bottom (m). There is at most one horizontal asymptote (HA).

\[f(x) = \frac{a_n x^n + \dots + a_0}{b_m x^m + \dots + b_0}\]
Degrees Horizontal asymptote Example
n < m (top smaller) y = 0 (the x-axis) 2x/(3x² + 1) → y = 0
n = m (equal) y = aₙ/bₘ (ratio of leading coefficients) 2x²/(x² − 1) → y = 2/1 = 2
n > m (top bigger) no HA (if n = m + 1 there is a slant asymptote) (x² − x)/(x + 1) → none

Leading-coefficient traps

  • The terms may be jumbled. In (3x³ + 7x² + 2)/(−2x³ + 16) the leading coefficients are 3 and −2, so the HA is y = −3/2.
  • Factored form hides the coefficient. In 3(x − 1)/(2x + 5) the HA is y = 3/2, not 3/1.
  • A backwards bracket flips the sign. In (x + 1)/(4 − x) the HA is y = 1/(−1) = −1.
  • Cancelling a common factor never changes the HA. You can use the original or the simplified function.

Can the graph cross the HA?

Yes. The HA only describes the far left and far right (x → ±∞). In the middle the graph may cross it; it can never cross a VA.

To check, set f(x) = the HA value and solve:

  • a real solution means the graph crosses at that x;
  • no solution means it never crosses;
  • if the solution is an excluded x (a hole), it does not cross there.
Situation Crosses? Example
HA y = 0 Yes, wherever the numerator is 0 (the x-intercepts) x/[(x + 1)(x − 2)] crosses at (0, 0)
Equal degrees, degree 2 or more Sometimes: solve (x² + x)/(x² − 4) = 1 gives x = −4, so it crosses at (−4, 1)
Linear over linear, (ax + b)/(cx + d) Never (x − 1)/(x − 3) = 1 gives −1 = −3, impossible
Transformed 1/x, A/(x − h) + k Never A/(x − h) = 0 has no solution

checks.q: Find the HA of f(x) = (5x² − 3)/(2 − x²).
Does f(x) = (x² − 3x)/(x² − 1) cross its HA? If so, where?
checks.ans: HA y = 1. x² − 3x = x² − 1 gives x = 1/3, so yes, it crosses at (1/3, 1)

sections.title: Slant (oblique) asymptotes
sections.html:
When the top's degree is exactly one more than the bottom's, the graph has a slant asymptote and no horizontal asymptote. Find it by long division: the quotient is the line, and the remainder is ignored.

\[f(x) = \frac{N(x)}{D(x)} = \underbrace{mx + c}_{\text{slant asymptote}} + \frac{r}{D(x)}\]

The fraction r/D(x) → 0 as x → ±∞, so the graph gets closer and closer to y = mx + c.

WorkedWorked example (Week 7, Example 12)

Divide x² − x by x + 1:

  1. x² ÷ x = x. Multiply: x(x + 1) = x² + x. Subtract: (x² − x) − (x² + x) = −2x.
  2. −2x ÷ x = −2. Multiply: −2(x + 1) = −2x − 2. Subtract: −2x − (−2x − 2) = 2.
\[\frac{x^2 - x}{x + 1} = x - 2 + \frac{2}{x + 1}\]

Slant asymptote y = x − 2; vertical asymptote x = −1.

Example 13: (x² − x − 2)/(x − 1) = x − 2/(x − 1), so the slant asymptote is y = x and the VA is x = 1. Intercepts: (0, 2), (−1, 0) and (2, 0).

Writing the remainder: when the left side is f(x)/d(x), the remainder goes over the divisor: q(x) + r(x)/d(x). When you multiply back out, it stands alone: f(x) = d(x)·q(x) + r(x).

checks.q: Find the slant and vertical asymptotes of g(x) = (2x² + 3x − 1)/(x + 2).

sections.title: Intercepts and sketching
sections.html:
Use the simplified function for intercepts. The x-intercepts come from the numerator, and the y-intercept is f(0).

  • x-intercepts: set the simplified numerator = 0. A constant numerator (e.g. 3/(x − 2)) means no x-intercept.
  • y-intercept: work out f(0). If x = 0 is not in the domain (e.g. (2x − 1)/x), there is no y-intercept.

The 7 steps from the notes

  1. Simplify f by factoring and cancelling. List any restrictions (holes).
  2. y-intercept: find and plot f(0), if it exists.
  3. x-intercepts: set the numerator = 0 and plot them.
  4. Vertical asymptotes and holes: set the denominator = 0. Draw VAs as dashed vertical lines and holes as open circles.
  5. Other asymptotes (horizontal or slant): draw them as dashed lines.
  6. Extra points: plot at least one point between, and one beyond, each x-intercept and VA.
  7. Join with smooth curves, approaching the asymptotes, never crossing a VA.

WorkedFully worked: Week 7, Example 11

\[f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 - 2x - 3} = \frac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{(x - 3)(x + 1)} = \frac{x + 3}{x + 1}, \quad x \neq 3\]
Step Result
1. Simplify (x + 3)/(x + 1), with x ≠ 3
2. y-intercept f(0) = 3/1 = 3, so (0, 3)
3. x-intercept x + 3 = 0, so (−3, 0)
4. VA and hole VA x = −1; hole at x = 3: y = 6/4 = 3/2, so (3, 3/2)
5. HA degrees equal: y = 1/1 = 1
6. Extra points f(−5) = 0.5, f(−2) = −1, f(−0.5) = 5, f(1) = 2, f(4) = 1.4
7. Shape Left of x = −1: comes from just below y = 1, through (−3, 0), down to −∞. Right of x = −1: from +∞ down through (0, 3), flattening towards y = 1, with a gap at (3, 1.5).

Check: (x + 3)/(x + 1) = 1 gives 3 = 1, which is impossible, so this graph never crosses its HA.

sections.title: Transformations of y = 1/x
sections.html:
Any function of the form A/(x − h) + k is the graph of 1/x moved and stretched. You can read its asymptotes straight off it: VA x = h and HA y = k.

\[g(x) = \frac{A}{x - h} + k\]
Part Effect on y = 1/x
(x − h), h > 0 shift h units right
(x + h), i.e. h < 0 shift left
+ k shift k units up (−k: down)
A < 0 reflect in the x-axis
|A| > 1 vertical stretch by |A|

WorkedExamples from the notes

Function Description VA HA
g(x) = −1/(x + 2) reflect in the x-axis, then shift 2 left x = −2 y = 0
h(x) = 1/(x − 1) + 3 shift 1 right, then 3 up x = 1 y = 3
g(x) = 3/(x − 2) = 3f(x − 2) vertical stretch by 3, shift 2 right x = 2 y = 0

For g(x) = 3/(x − 2): the y-intercept is (0, −3/2); there is no x-intercept because 3 ≠ 0. Extra points: g(1) = −3, g(3) = 3, g(5) = 1.

sections.title: Exam checklist, traps and practice
sections.html:
For any rational function in the test, run through this list in order.

  • Domain from the original denominator
  • Factor and cancel; any cancelled factor is a hole (find its y from the simplified function)
  • VA from the simplified denominator
  • HA from the degree rule, or slant asymptote by long division if n = m + 1
  • x-intercepts (simplified numerator = 0) and y-intercept f(0)
  • Sketch: dashed asymptotes, open circle for the hole, extra points either side of each VA

Traps that lose marks

  • Calling a cancelled factor a VA. It is a hole.
  • Missing a negative leading coefficient, e.g. in (4 − x).
  • Writing "HA y = 0" when the degrees are equal.
  • Drawing the curve across a VA. It never crosses; it may cross the HA.
  • Forgetting that a constant numerator means no x-intercept.

Practice questions (answers below — cover them first)

  1. f(x) = (x² − x − 6)/(x² − 4). Find the domain, hole, asymptotes and intercepts.
  2. Find the HA of f(x) = (5x² − 3)/(2 − x²).
  3. Find the slant and vertical asymptotes of g(x) = (2x² + 3x − 1)/(x + 2).
  4. Does f(x) = (x² − 3x)/(x² − 1) cross its HA? If so, where?
  5. Describe h(x) = 2/(x + 1) − 3 compared with y = 1/x, and give its asymptotes and intercepts.
  6. Find the domain and asymptotes of f(x) = (x + 5)/(x² + 4).

Answers

Q Answer
1 (x − 3)(x + 2)/[(x − 2)(x + 2)] = (x − 3)/(x − 2). Domain ℝ \ {−2, 2}; hole (−2, 5/4); VA x = 2; HA y = 1; intercepts (3, 0) and (0, 3/2)
2 Leading coefficients 5 and −1, so y = −5
3 2x² + 3x − 1 = (x + 2)(2x − 1) + 1, so g(x) = 2x − 1 + 1/(x + 2). Slant y = 2x − 1, VA x = −2
4 HA y = 1. x² − 3x = x² − 1 gives x = 1/3, so yes, it crosses at (1/3, 1)
5 Vertical stretch by 2, shift 1 left, 3 down. VA x = −1, HA y = −3. y-intercept (0, −1); x-intercept: 2/(x + 1) = 3 gives x = −1/3, so (−1/3, 0)
6 x² + 4 is never 0, so the domain is all reals and there is no VA. Degree 1 < 2, so HA y = 0
